top.title: Senate passes bills establishing research fund, granting medical college PhD powers
top.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — The Senate has passed two bills seeking to provide a framework for research funding and expand postgraduate medical education in Nigeria. The bills are the National Research and Innovation Development Fund Establishment Bill, 2026, and the National Postgraduate Medical College Act Amendment Bill, 2026. Both bills were passed on Wednesday after consideration of their provisions, clause by clause, at the Committee of the Whole and subsequent third reading. Their passage followed the presentation and consideration of reports by the Senate Committee on Tertiary Institutions and TETFund, chaired by Senator Mohammed Dandutse (APC, Katsina South). Presenting the reports, Dandutse said the National Research and Innovation Development Fund Establishment Bill sought to establish a sustainable funding mechanism for research, development and innovation across the country. He said the proposed legislation also provided for the establishment of the National Council on Research and Innovation, which would provide strategic direction, policy oversight and supervision for Nigeria’s research agenda. According to him, the proposed fund would support research institutions and provide a dedicated funding framework for addressing the country’s development challenges. He added that the fund and the council would work together to strengthen Nigeria’s research, scientific, technological and innovation capabilities. On the National Postgraduate Medical College Act Amendment Bill, Dandutse said the proposed amendment sought to expand the academic and institutional functions of the college. He explained that the amendment would empower the college to establish academic programmes and award Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) degrees in specialised medical disciplines. The areas include clinical medicine, dentistry, basic medical sciences, pharmacology and other related fields. Dandutse further explained that the amendment would empower the college’s Senate to develop, administer and supervise the proposed doctoral programmes. He said the programmes would be subject to accreditation and regulation by the National Universities Commission (NUC) to ensure compliance with prescribed academic standards. According to him, the proposed changes are intended to provide a framework for advanced medical education, clinical research and specialised medical training in the country. top.title: MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof
top.description: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform. The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications. It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability. Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency. Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price. But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users? In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure." The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support. MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together. MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part. Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level. SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system. top.title: 'A shotgun marriage': Why are NASA’s SkyFall Mars helicopters riding on a nuclear rocket?
top.description: null The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket. NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet . But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the " Mars Czar ") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'" Shotgun marriage? Hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform. Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management issues." Since the SkyFall mission concept first appeared, he said, the usual sequence for a science mission is reversed. "The science community is having to scramble to back into a set of requirements and objectives that match the SkyFall capabilities. Fortunately the community is very creative," said Hubbard, "and the basic Planetary Decadal objectives are very broad." top.title: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
top.description: United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply. "ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday," the company said in a statement . "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket's failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle's main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. nigeria.title: World Bank threatened to cut Nigeria’s financing over subsidy — Fashola
nigeria.description: Former Lagos State Governor, Babatunde Fashola, has said the World Bank warned Nigeria that it would stop financing the country unless the Federal Government removed petrol subsidy. Fashola, who served as Minister of Power under the late President Muhammadu Buhari, made the disclosure on Tuesday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today. He said the decision to remove the subsidy was not merely a policy choice, but was also influenced by legal provisions and Nigeria’s financial position at the time. Fashola urged Nigerians to revisit President Bola Tinubu’s inaugural address, arguing that public attention had focused largely on the declaration that “subsidy is gone” without sufficient consideration of other parts of the speech. He also cited the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA), which he said provided for petroleum products to be sold at competitive market rates, arguing that the provision had implications for any move to reinstate subsidy. “The World Bank simply said, ‘We won’t finance your country again unless you remove subsidy.’ It was that simple,” he said. Fashola said the issue had been discussed during the previous administration, when he was a member of the Federal Executive Council, adding that Nigeria was spending close to 90 per cent of its revenue on debt servicing. He argued that the country could not afford to sustain the subsidy regime and challenged those advocating its restoration to explain how they intended to fund it. The former minister also asked political opponents of the Tinubu administration to explain how they would implement an alternative policy if elected, saying some politicians who had previously supported subsidy removal had changed their positions after it became unpopular. He said the Tinubu administration deserved commendation for maintaining the policy despite the economic difficulties it had imposed on Nigerians. “What this government deserves commendation for is not falling over on its word and saying, ‘Because the people like it, let’s bring it back.’ It was a road to perdition,” he said. Fashola, however, acknowledged that subsidy removal had affected household livelihoods and increased the cost of living, but said the government was introducing other measures to cushion the impact. He listed tax reforms, the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), salary adjustments and compressed natural gas (CNG) initiatives among the measures being deployed to address the economic pressures. He also cited a decline in inflation from above 30 per cent to about 14 per cent, arguing that reversing the subsidy policy midway could disrupt the progress recorded. nigeria.description: …Says students, beneficiaries would revolt against such proposal Former Lagos State Governor, Babatunde Fashola, has challenged opposition politicians to campaign on a promise to scrap the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), saying beneficiaries and their families would resist such a move. Fashola, who spoke on Tuesday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today, described the student loan scheme introduced by President Bola Tinubu’s administration as one of the reforms that had eased the financial burden on families across the country. NELFUND was established in April 2024 after Tinubu signed the Student Loans (Access to Higher Education) Act into law to provide interest-free loans to eligible students in tertiary institutions. nigeria.description: By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse At least three people have been killed and two others injured in a violent clash involving suspected herders and farmers in Garki Local Government Area of Jigawa State. The incident reportedly occurred at about 3:30 a.m. on Wednesday at Wauta Fulani Settlement in Rafin Marke Ward, Kanya District. The Jigawa State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) confirmed the incident in a statement issued on Wednesday by its Public Relations Officer, ASC Badruddeen Tijjani Mahmud. According to the corps, preliminary investigations indicated that seven suspected herders, accompanied by about 200 cattle from the Babura axis, allegedly entered a farmland belonging to 53-year-old Amadu Saleh, where the animals fed on his guinea corn crops. The statement said efforts by farmers to prevent further destruction of their crops reportedly triggered an attack by the suspected herders, who allegedly wielded cutlasses, bows and arrows. The confrontation resulted in the death of 35-year-old Amiru Saleh, while Amadu Saleh, 50, and Haruna Saleh, 37, sustained injuries. The NSCDC said another confrontation subsequently occurred after other farmers gathered at the scene, leading to the deaths of two unidentified members of the herders’ group. The surviving members of the group reportedly fled with their cattle towards Gabasawa Local Government Area of neighbouring Kano State. The corps said all the victims were taken to Garki General Hospital, where the three deceased persons were confirmed dead. It added that the remains of Amiru Saleh had been released to his relatives for burial, while the bodies of the two unidentified persons remained at the hospital pending necessary official procedures. Reacting to the incident, the NSCDC State Commandant, CC Muhammad Kabiru Ingawa, appealed to residents to avoid retaliatory attacks and refrain from taking the law into their own hands. He urged members of the affected communities to remain calm and promptly report suspicious activities or potential security threats to relevant authorities. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine Coinbase Says Its AI Blocked $4.7 Million in Deepfake Elon Musk Scam Coinbase (COIN) said its AI scam-prevention agent stopped about $4.7 million in customer funds from reaching scammers who used a deepfake of Elon Musk to pitch a fake Tesla crypto giveaway, blocking roughly 91% of the money customers tried to send. The exchange described the incident in a Tuesday blog post, part of a weekly series on consumer protection. It said the system worked “with no humans in the loop.” Those two figures imply customers tried to send about $5.2 million, and that roughly $460,000 still left their accounts. Coinbase did not say how much reached the scammers. A livestream that wasn’t real The scam ran during Tesla’s “flying car” demo. Scammers set up a YouTube livestream that looked like the real broadcast, with a deepfake Musk, on-screen wallet addresses and a QR code. The stream promised to double any crypto sent to it, and more than half a million people watched, Coinbase said. Over about two hours, hundreds of Coinbase customers tried to send millions of dollars to the addresses on screen. Many were long-time users. Coinbase did not say when the fake stream ran or which coins customers tried to send. The company stressed that its platform was not breached. “Nobody was hacked,” Coinbase wrote. “No Coinbase account was broken into, no password stolen, no credential phished.” That is what makes giveaway fraud hard to stop, since most defenses look for activity the account holder did not authorize, and here the customers logged in and pressed confirm themselves. “Our systems can see risk signals in real time. They can’t see intent,” the post said. How the agent works Coinbase said its defense has three parts. Machine learning models first score outgoing sends in real time, watching for giveaway patterns, brand impersonation and newly created wallet addresses. The goal, the company wrote, is “to catch the danger, not the customer.” When a send is flagged, a scam-specific agent takes over, looking up context, naming the scam pattern, explaining how giveaway schemes work and asking questions meant to make the story fall apart. Each reply is scored for confidence before the customer sees it, so the system knows when a situation needs more friction. The agent had never been trained on this kind of con, Coinbase said. Deepfake giveaways tied to a live product launch were not in its training data. “It recognized the shape of the scheme anyway,” the company wrote, pointing to the promise to multiply funds, the deadline of a live event and a transfer that could not be reversed. Cheaper fakes Coinbase said deepfakes have changed the economics of the scam. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine New York State Pension Fund Boosts Strategy (MSTR) Stake by More Than 10% The New York State Common Retirement Fund raised its stake in Strategy (MSTR) by more than 10% in the third quarter, to 352,850 shares worth $54.0 million at Sept. 30. The pension fund disclosed the position in a Form 13F filed Tuesday, covering the quarter ended Sept. 30. It added 33,000 shares from the 319,850 it reported at June 30. That is an increase of a little more than 10%. The filing does not say why the pension fund added the shares. The reported value nearly doubled, to $54.0 million from $27.8 million. Strategy’s stock closed the quarter at $153.09, up from $86.93 at midyear, so most of the gain in dollar value came from the rally, not from the added shares. A small slice of a large pension fund The fund is one of the largest public pension plans in the U.S. It holds the assets used to pay retirement benefits for New York’s state and local public employees. Comptroller Thomas P. DiNapoli, the fund’s trustee, valued it at an estimated $309.7 billion as of June 30, the latest official figure. There is not yet a published valuation for Sept. 30. Public equities are only part of the portfolio. As of March 31, they accounted for 39.4% of the fund’s assets, with the rest in cash and bonds, private equity, real estate and other alternatives. The 13F lists 2,975 holdings worth $71.3 billion. The Strategy stake is a small slice of that book, less than a tenth of a percent. Strategy has made bitcoin its primary treasury asset. The company held 850,849 bitcoin as of Nov. 15, with an aggregate purchase price of $64.20 billion, or $75,452 a coin. Institutional managers have 45 days after quarter-end to file a 13F. Tuesday’s report is the first official look at the pension fund’s third-quarter buying, after the stock had already fallen sharply from the $153.09 price used in the filing. Strategy shares have already fallen Strategy closed Tuesday at $96.50, below $100 and about 37% under its Sept. 30 close. At that price, the same 352,850 shares are worth about $34 million, roughly $20 million less than the value in the filing. The common shares also finished under Strategy’s STRC preferred stock, which closed at $98.70. That is the first time they have closed below the preferred since mid-August. The stock is down about 20% from its Nov. 10 close of $121.07. A 13F is a snapshot. It does not show whether the pension fund bought or sold shares in October or November, when most of that decline took place. Coinbase and miners, but no bitcoin ETFs The information table lists no shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust or other spot bitcoin ETFs, and no shares of Strategy’s preferred stock. The pension fund does hold Coinbase (COIN). It reported 109,433 shares at Sept. 30, a little below the 111,633 shares it held at midyear. The reported value still rose, to $20.4 million from $16.3 million, as Coinbase’s stock climbed. It also holds a string of bitcoin miners.

business.description: Bitcoin Magazine South Korea Set to Let 3,500 Companies Buy Bitcoin, Report Says South Korea’s Financial Services Commission plans to publish guidelines next week that would let about 3,500 listed companies and professional-investor firms buy bitcoin and other crypto for investment, a local news agency reported Wednesday. The guidelines will be released alongside the government’s draft of the Digital Asset Basic Act, the country’s planned framework for the crypto industry, according to the report . The FSC plans to convene its Virtual Asset Committee to coincide with the release. The FSC itself has not publicly announced a date for either release. If it lands next week, the move would come one year and nine months after the regulator laid out its roadmap for corporate crypto access in February 2025. A roadmap that stalled That plan opened the market in stages, with nonprofits and crypto service providers coming first, and only to sell. Since June 2025, Korean nonprofits have been able to cash out crypto they receive as donations, and World Vision made the first such trade, selling donated ether on Upbit. Exchanges have also been allowed to sell their own holdings to cover operating costs. Coinone and DigitalX, formerly Korbit, have done so several times after filing disclosures. The second stage, which lets listed companies and firms registered as professional investors trade crypto for investment, was slated for the second half of 2025. It never arrived. The holdup is market plumbing. Corporate orders are large, and even Korea’s biggest exchanges have limited room to absorb them without moving prices. “If companies come into the market and trade 5 billion won each, even an exchange like Upbit would struggle to take that volume,” an unnamed industry official told News1. Large trades would normally run through over-the-counter desks, and Korea does not yet have rules governing how those desks operate. What the Basic Act adds The Digital Asset Basic Act is meant to close that gap. It would split crypto service providers into separate business types and set entry and conduct rules for OTC desks, brokers and other operators, the report said. The government’s draft is expected to go to the National Assembly next week. Lawmakers want it passed quickly. The Assembly’s Political Affairs Committee aims to process the bill by January, timed to the implementation of the U.S. GENIUS Act, the stablecoin law. Rep. entertainment.description: Beyoncé becomes the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram If you have ever wondered what triple digits look like on music’s biggest stage, Beyoncé just gave everyone the answer. The Houston-born global music superstar has officially become the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations, hitting the milestone with her latest nod for “ Morning Dew ( Donk )”, which is nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards (2027 Grammys). Released in July 2026 ahead of the 20th anniversary of her sophomore album B’Day, “Morning Dew (Donk)” puts her in a category alongside Kehlani , Victoria Monét , Jill Scott , and Nigerian star Tems . To put the 100-nomination milestone into perspective, no other recording artist has ever crossed into triple digits since the Grammys began. Beyoncé had previously been tied with her husband, Jay-Z , at 88 nominations each before breaking that tie in 2024 with 11 nods for Cowboy Carter to reach 99—and this latest recognition pushes her even further ahead as the artist with the highest number of Grammy nominations in history. Beyoncé holding her three Grammy trophies at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards in 2025. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram It is also a good reminder of how long she has been doing this at the highest level. Beyoncé’s Grammy journey started all the way back in 2000 as part of Destiny’s Child with “Bills, Bills, Bills”, and across more than two decades as a solo artist, group member, and collaborator, she has built a record that keeps stretching further ahead of the pack. Alongside holding the title for the most Grammy nominations of all time, she is already the most awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins, a record she first broke in 2023 when she surpassed late conductor Georg Solti ’s 31 trophies. Now all eyes turn to Sunday, 7 February 2027, when the 2027 Grammy Awards take place at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles and we find out whether nomination number 100 turns into Grammy win number 36. Was I considerate? Did I treat him well? Could I have done something differently? I caught myself wondering whether I should have given him a chance . Perhaps I should have allowed him to love me. entertainment.title: Visa Report Identifies Opportunity to Integrate Digital Payments with SMEs Business Operations in Nigeria
entertainment.description: Report identifies next SME digitization opportunity: connecting payments with day-to-day business management. 94% of SMEs surveyed find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, yet only 29% currently use one, pointing to untapped demand for tools that connect payments with business management. Integrated payment and business solutions can give financial institutions a more holistic view of SME cash flow and support more tailored financing solutions over time. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nigeria have largely moved beyond the first stage of digital payment adoption, but a productivity gap remains. According to Visa’s new survey for its Pay and Get Paid 2026 report, most of the SMEs surveyed in Nigeria use digital payments, showing how firmly digital commerce has taken root in the country’s small business economy. However, many SMEs still manage the related financial and operational tasks separately, with only 29% currently using an integrated solution that connects payments with broader business management. The report shows that financial admin and disconnected tools create friction for SMEs, with surveyed businesses citing challenges in tracking outstanding invoices (14%), keeping payroll records organized (19%), and preparing financial reports (16%). These pain points reflect a disconnect between payments and the operational tasks that follow, with some businesses juggling multiple systems to keep their business running. The appetite for a more connected approach is clear. According to the report, 94% of SMEs find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, reflecting strong interest in tools that can bring payments and key business operations into one experience. However, adoption has yet to catch up: only 29% of SMEs currently use an integrated payment and business platform. The report points to several perception barriers that may be slowing adoption. Businesses cited that they already have manual processes that work (8%), that an integrated platform may disrupt their current way of working (8%), or that they do not trust relying on a single provider (7%). These findings suggest that broader adoption will depend on helping SMEs better understand how integrated tools can be relevant, accessible, and scalable for businesses at different stages of growth. At the same time, the experience of SMEs already using integrated solutions suggests a strong value case. The report found that Nigerian businesses using an integrated tool or platform report 93% satisfaction, with 88% reporting efficiency gains, including reductions in the time and effort required to manage their business. Beyond efficiency, integrated platforms may also create new opportunities for financial institutions to deepen SME relationships by using richer payments and business-management data to better understand cash flow patterns, support risk assessment, and potentially enable more relevant lending solutions over time. entertainment.description: Sade Adu in the Performer category and Fela Kuti in the Early Influence category, both inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Class of 2026. Nigerian music history just added another major chapter in Los Angeles, and the celebration has been loud from Lagos to London. On Saturday, 14 November 2026, Afrobeat pioneer Fela Aníkúlápó Kuti and Nigerian-British singer Sade Adu were officially inducted into the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame during a star-studded ceremony at the Peacock Theatre. For Fela Kuti, nearly three decades after his passing in 1997, this induction makes him the first African-born solo artist to enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Honoured posthumously in the Early Influence category—five years after he was first nominated in 2021—the recognition celebrates how he fused West African rhythms with jazz, funk, and soul to create Afrobeat, using his voice and horns to confront social and political injustice across classics like “Zombie”, “Water No Get Enemy”, and “Sorrow, Tears and Blood”. It also caps off an extraordinary 2026 for his legacy, coming just months after the Recording Academy presented him with a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in February, another first for an African artist. From left, Made Kuti, Femi Kuti, Yeni Kuti, and Seun Kuti in Los Angeles for Fela Aníkúlápó Kuti’s posthumous induction into the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Photo Credit: Femi Kuti/Instagram Representing the Afrobeat legend on the night were members of the Kuti family, with his children Yeni Kuti , Femi Kuti , Seun Kuti , and Shalewa Kuti , alongside his grandson Made Kuti , stepping out in Los Angeles to accept the honour on his behalf. Speaking on the milestone, the family reflected on how remarkable it is to see Fela receive both the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and a Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction in the very same year. Meanwhile, Sade Adu —born Helen Folasade Adu in Ibadan—was inducted in th e Performer category as the frontwoman of her acclaimed British band Sade , alongside longtime bandmates Stuart Matthewman , Paul Spencer Denman , and Andrew Hale . Earning their spot on their second nomination, the group behind timeless soul-jazz records such as “Smooth Operator”, “The Sweetest Taboo”, and “Your Love Is King” opted to sit out the ceremony in true low-key fashion, though they shared a warm message thanking fans and dedicating the milestone to their late longtime producer Mike Pela . entertainment.description: Tems receiving the Best African Music Performance at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards. In June 2023, ahead of the 66th Grammy Awards, the Recording Academy announced the creation of the Best African Music Performance category. Its creation was a recognition of how far African music had travelled globally, and Nigerian artists were at the centre of that movement. From Burna Boy ‘s Ye , CKay ‘s Love Nwantiti , Wizkid ‘s explosive Essence , to Rema ‘s globally successful Calm Down and others, Nigerian artists became drivers of African music’s global expansion. Afrobeats – the umbrella term often used internationally to describe much of contemporary African popular music, although many Nigerian artists have rejected it for its tendency to limit the range of music coming out of the country – became an established genre globally. While Nigerian and African music have always travelled beyond their respective countries, the era of streaming and digital platforms has accelerated how quickly global audiences discover and engage with the music. African music became increasingly established in the West and other parts of the world, creating greater recognition for its artists and sounds. The Grammys’ decision to introduce a category specifically recognising African music performances was an important step in that direction, beyond the recognition African artists had previously received in categories such as Best Global Music Album. Although the creation of the Best African Music Performance category was celebrated throughout the continent, there seems to be a monopoly, or something close to it, of Nigerian music in the category. While South African artist Tyla has won the award twice, more than any individual Nigerian artist, Nigerian artists have consistently enjoyed greater representation in the nominations. Indeed, Nigerian artists are considerably more recognised globally, particularly in the West. However, I believe it is the responsibility of an award of this repute to look beyond the most visible names and recognise the best African music released within its eligibility period. entertainment.title: Tems Is Officially a 12-Time Grammy Nominee!
entertainment.description: Tems is officially a 12-time Grammy nominee after securing four nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards. Photo Credit: Tems/Instagram One, two, three… and now 12! Tems has added four more Grammy nominations to her record, bringing her career total to 12 ahead of the 69th Grammy Awards. The latest recognition also makes her the first Nigerian female artist to receive four nominations in a single Grammy year, with this year’s shortlist recognising her work across four categories. The Nigerian singer is in contention for Best Global Music Album with her 10-track EP, Love Is a Kingdom , and Best African Music Performance for “ Big Daddy ”. She has also earned nominations for Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song for “ What You Need ”. The four nominations give her one of the most extensive Nigerian representations at this year’s ceremony and bring her Grammy wins to two, following previous victories in 2023 and 2025. Her relationship with the Recording Academy began in 2022, when she received her first nomination for her contribution to Wizkid ‘s “ Essence ”, which was nominated for Best Global Music Performance at the 64th Grammy Awards. The following year brought three more nominations, this time for her work on Future’s “ Wait for U ” featuring Drake and Beyoncé ‘s Renaissance . She won her first Grammy that night, taking home Best Melodic Rap Performance for “Wait for U”, while also receiving nominations for Album of the Year and Best Rap Song. Tems earned another nomination at the 66th Grammy Awards in 2024 for “ Lift Me Up ”, her contribution to the Black Panther : Wakanda Forever soundtrack, in the Best Song Written for Visual Media category. She returned to the Grammys the following year with three nominations, including Best Global Music Album for her debut album, Born in the Wild , and Best R&B Song for “ Burning ”. Her second Grammy win came in the Best African Music Performance category, where “ Love Me JeJe ” took home the award at the 67th Grammy Awards in February 2025. technology.title: MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof
technology.description: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform. The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications. It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability. Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency. Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price. But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users? In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure." The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support. MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together. MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part. Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level. SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system. technology.title: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
technology.description: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021 . Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next. The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds. Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex , the familiar list of requirements came up first: Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching. Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise. Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled. So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it. Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones. Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000. Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully. technology.title: PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road
technology.description: Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement. It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, " be removed from a future version of Windows ," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default. After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties. PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless. PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover , who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude. PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain. The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time. Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts. Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft. Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself. "Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead. Microsoft says PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®

In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. technology.title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
technology.description: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. Sponsored by Infinidat

technology.title: Space robot legend Voyager 1 is now more than 1 light-day away
technology.description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there. Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union. A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto. Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good. Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs). Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register : "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it. "We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with." Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said. Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

technology.title: StubHub International warns customer data may have left the venue
technology.description: Ticket resale giant StubHub International has warned customers that a recent breach may have exposed their personal information to cybercriminals. The company said it detected "unauthorized access to certain systems" on its platform between late October and early November. Customer notification emails seen by The Register list potentially affected information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and country or regional settings. StubHub International, operated by Ticketbis S.L., apologized for the intrusion and offered the usual promise to implement security enhancements after the fact. The company said it had addressed "certain vulnerabilities" while containing the incident and was continuing to monitor for suspicious activity. Outside cybersecurity experts are assisting with the ongoing investigation. The company warned that any exposed information could be used to make subsequent scams more convincing. "To date, we have found no evidence of unauthorised access to account passwords , banking information or payment card details," the email stated. "We also have no evidence that the compromised information has been used fraudulently. "However, there is a risk that third parties could use this information to attempt fraud, identity theft or phishing through emails, messages or calls that appear to come from StubHub International or other trusted organizations." The Register contacted StubHub International for more information, such as how many customers were affected, but it did not respond. Digital Fuel Capital bought StubHub International from Viagogo in 2021 after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) required the international business to be sold to address competition concerns. In June, the CMA fined Ticketbis £889,200 and ordered refunds exceeding £590,000 after finding that mandatory fees were omitted from upfront ticket prices. technology.title: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share

We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them. Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them. Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case. In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow , an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon. NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet . But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the " Mars Czar ") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'" Shotgun marriage? Hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform. Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management issues." science.description: Reconstruction of a specimen of Homo erectus S. ENTRESSANGLE/E. DAYNES/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY Preserved teeth from two caves in southern China indicate Homo erectus lived on mainland Asia as recently as 184,000 years ago. That is recent enough for the species to have met later groups like the Denisovans. It seems these Chinese H. erectus were living in a tropical rainforest – an environment where the species has not previously been found. “We’ve got this late surviving population, and we’ve got this rich story of how they were living,” says geochronologist Kira Westaway at Macquarie University in Sydney. Advertisement H. erectus was one of the first species in our genus, Homo . It was also the first species of hominin we know for sure migrated beyond Africa. The earliest H. erectus fossils are from Africa 2 million years ago, but by 1.8 million years ago they were living in what is now Georgia on the border between Europe and Asia. Eventually the species spread further east into what is now China. They even made it to the island of Java. Read more The 85-million-year timeline of human evolution The most recent fossils identified as H. erectus are from Java and are between 117,000 and 108,000 years old . However, it’s been thought the species vanished much earlier from mainland Asia. Until the discoveries from China announced today, the most recent securely dated H. erectus were from around 400,000 years ago. Around this time, other hominin groups emerged, like the Denisovans who lived in East Asia. “The assumption would have been that erectus is basically no longer there, because they have evolved into a Denisovan population,” says molecular palaeontologist Frido Welker at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark. Welker, Westaway and their colleagues investigated two caves in southern China. Baxian and Naxian are both limestone caves, about 15 kilometres apart. They were initially excavated by Chinese teams led by Yingqi Zhang at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing and Wei Wang at Shandong University. science.description: NIST’s campus in Boulder, Colorado NIST Financial institutions and critical infrastructure could be made far more secure in the near-future using quantum particles. For years, researchers have predicted that quantum particles could enable someone to share their location, and to verify someone else’s, in a way that is exceedingly difficult to hack. This would allow one branch of a bank to confirm that a request for funds or client information is coming from another branch and not from a hacker. Likewise, hackers could be stopped from trying to remotely control a power grid, a nuclear plant – or even commercial freezers, which have recently been hacked across Europe . Gautam Kavuri at the University of Colorado Boulder and his colleagues have now shown that quantum devices really can provide such location verification, offering a level of security impenetrable to most hackers. Advertisement Read more Inside the company selling quantum entanglement “From a security perspective, it’s sort of the gold-plated Rolls Royce of protocols. It’s got the best security you can have in principle, while making the least assumptions,” says team member Krister Shalm at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Colorado. “And you can actually do it.” In the researchers’ experiment, two verifier devices had to confirm the location of a third device called the prover. Each device was in a different location: the verifiers were 195 metres apart in different labs and the prover was in a third location between them. Kavuri says it was important for these devices to be in different rooms on the NIST campus, rather than all in the same lab, because this is closer to a practical scenario in the real world. The devices were connected with electrical cables and optical fibres and could exchange quantum particles of light that had been connected into pairs through the inextricable link of quantum entanglement . To begin the new quantum position verification (QPV) protocol, a verifier would send one photon from an entangled pair to the prover and, simultaneously, each verifier would also send a random number that instructed the prover on which particle property to measure. Next, the prover sent the outcome of that measurement to both verifiers. They used the time it took to receive this information to calculate the prover’s position. First, quantum information, such as that carried by particles of light, can never be copied or cloned surreptitiously . Additionally, the researchers leveraged a procedure called a Bell test , which is specific to entangled particles, and would be failed if a hacker tampered with them. The net effect was that any conventional strategy for faking the position would set off one of these quantum safeguards. science.description: Artist’s impression of a large star absorbing the matter of another Nazarii_Neshcherenskyi/Shutterstock For the first time, astronomers have seen a star expand and gobble up its stellar companion. Watching this process as it happened has given researchers crucial insights into the evolution of stars that they have been seeking for decades. In early 2025, a group of researchers reported that a star in the Andromeda galaxy had been gradually brightening since 2018 – an interesting finding, but not one that was particularly unusual. But later in the year, the SPHEREx space telescope serendipitously caught that same object, which turned out to be a stellar binary , in an extraordinary outburst: over the course of about a month, it expanded at a rate of 330 kilometres per second and flashed with light 100 times brighter than it had emitted before. That was far more unusual. Viraj Karambelkar at Columbia University in New York and his colleagues followed up on the object, named AT 2025abao, with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and analysed all of the available data together. They found that AT 2025abao was undergoing a process we knew stars must go through, but had never seen before, in which a red giant star expands and engulfs its smaller companion, which spirals towards the core of the larger star and is eventually ripped to shreds . Advertisement Read more Impossibly fast-moving stars are revealing the Milky Way’s mysterious heart “We were able to see all different phases of this process – we were able to see the quiescent system, we were able to see the moment the stars touched each other, we were able to see the inspiral, and we were able to see the big outburst in 2025,” says Karambelkar. “So we now know how this process works far better than we ever had before.” The outburst came from the moment that the smaller star, which the research team nicknamed Small Bao, was ripped apart at the core of the larger star, Big Bao. This series of events is called the common envelope phase, and the fact that it takes only a few years of a star’s billions-of-years lifespan makes it a rare process, and one that is challenging to observe. “This is probably the most uncertain and critical phase in the evolution of a star,” says Jason Nordhaus at the Rochester Institute of Technology in New York state, who was not involved in this research. Nearly one-third of stars will go through this phase at some point in their lifetimes, more if you consider those that engulf other objects that are not stars, such as planets , he says. (Image credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Acknowledgment: PIs: G. Narayan & T. Murphey (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign) Image processing: M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)) A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth. What is it? Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf . During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion. Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter. This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place. Why is it incredible? Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres. ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system. But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova. Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time. SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a " thermometer for Earth " in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence , the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says. "It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview. That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs. The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches . Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai. "We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth ," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO. First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology. Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. science.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
science.description: null NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later. "The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance." All things Voyager The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond. On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn. "Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries. science.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 18 – A… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Medium-Sized Solar Flare Explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations , meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays . M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares ! NASA, NOAA , and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space. A moisture-laden storm delivered heavy rains to lower elevations in the Sacramento area and snow accumulations of around a foot to some mountainous areas. The recent bout of wet weather was the first in a quick succession of Pacific storms bringing rain, snow, and wind to the U.S. West in mid-November. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured this image (right) of fresh snow in the Sierra Nevada on the morning of November 14, during a lull between weather systems. Two days earlier (left), the mountains were mostly bare, with snow appearing only at the highest elevations. Nearly 12 inches (30 centimeters) of snow fell at Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, on November 13, according to the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory . The accumulation snarled traffic on Interstate 80 in the area, prompting officials to close the highway in both directions that evening. To the south, the ski resort at Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches (23 to 33 centimeters) of new snow, and officials at Yosemite National Park closed several roads ahead of the storm. More wet weather and mountain snow are forecast to follow . The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a winter storm warning for portions of the Sierras above 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) in elevation from November 18 to 20. NWS warned of difficult-to-impossible travel conditions, gusty winds, and snow accumulations of around 4 feet (120 centimeters) possible above 8,000 feet (2,400 meters). science.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
science.description: The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge Credit: NASA / David Lam NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight. “As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!” Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable. Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space. Judges Needed NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers website . science.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
science.description: null Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA . Need for speed The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9. The trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2 through the outer solar system. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much. "Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote . "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure." science.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
science.description: 2 min read NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records Two NASA Space Apps Challenge participants in Vilhena, Brazil work together during the annual hackathon on their project submission. NASA On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation. Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries. The challenge provides an opportunity for hands-on experience with NASA science, mobilizing an engaged global community of technologists and space science enthusiasts to answer questions that benefit humanity and drive exploration. Participants join events organized by local volunteers to work in teams and address one of the challenges and submit their project before the deadline. Projects are then judged to determine 10 global winners, to be announced in January. “The Space Apps Challenge invites people with many different skillsets to leverage NASA’s gold-standard datasets to address real challenges facing us here on Earth and in space,” said Amy Kaminski, engagement branch chief, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We’re thrilled to see more than 180,000 people tackling these challenges and helping to accelerate our ability to find solutions.” One of the local winning teams from NASA Space Apps Challenge NYC pose with volunteer local lead Nate Cooper. NASA Challenges also feature data from 17 international space agency partners, all Artemis Accord signatories. This year’s space agency partners are: Angola National Space Programme Management Office (GGPEN), Bahrain Space Agency, Brazilian Space Agency (AEB), CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation), Italian Space Agency, JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), KASA (Korea AeroSpace Administration), Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Center of the United Arab Emirates, National Space Activities Commission of Argentina (CONAE), Nigeria’s National Space Research and Development Agency, Paraguayan Space Agency, Senegalese Space Studies Agency, Spanish Space Agency, Turkish Space Agency, and UK Space Agency. Three agencies, GGPEN, AEB, and CONAE, also wrote challenges this year.
